### Pass 94 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Compute the Verdier/solid dual of the all-prime Borel $j_!$ coefficient and
decide exactly what remains of the finite signed functional equation.

Proposer:
Pass 93 turned the all-prime Borel coefficient into
$$
\mathfrak B^{\mathrm{cont}}_{j!}
=\mathbb Q^\times\ltimes
R\!\varprojlim_{S\Subset\mathbb P}j_{S,!}\mathcal V_S,
$$
whose unipotent cohomology is
$$
\epsilon=\widehat{\mathbb Z}/\mathbb Z.
$$
Therefore the solid dual is forced by Passes 77--79:
$$
D\epsilon\simeq\mathbb Q[-1],
\qquad
D\mathbb Q\simeq\epsilon[-1].
$$
The dual of the unipotent part is not an opposite unipotent group in degree
$0$; it is the degree-$1$ finite-adele boundary represented by
$$
0\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb A_f\to\epsilon\to0.
$$
Keeping the global Levi, the dual Borel shadow is consequently a
Levi-marked boundary object
$$
\mathbb Q^\times\ltimes\mathbb Q[-1],
$$
with the $\mathbb Q^\times$ action contragredient to the action on
$\epsilon$.  This is the all-prime continuation of the finite Verdier rule
$$
D(d_S)=-d_S^T.
$$
So the antipode sign does survive, but only as a signed boundary equation.

Skeptic:
The word "functional equation" is dangerous here.  In a usual principal
series, the functional equation is carried by a Weyl/Fourier intertwiner.  The
solid phantom line has no such degree-$0$ operator:
$$
\operatorname{Hom}^0_{\mathrm{Solid}}(\epsilon,\mathbb Q)=0.
$$
Equivalently, the opposite unipotent
$\bar U=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Solid}}(\epsilon,\mathbb Q)$ remains zero.
Thus Pass 94 must not say that the Borel coefficient has acquired an
$s\mapsto -s$ intertwiner or a genuine Weyl flip.  The finite shadows still
see $d_S\mapsto-d_S^T$, and the all-prime object still has biduality sign
$-\mathrm{id}_\epsilon$, but the honest statement is boundary-level:
the missing flip is replaced by the shifted Ext class, not repaired.

Formalist:
> **Theorem 94a (solid dual of the all-prime unipotent).** Let
> $\epsilon=\widehat{\mathbb Z}/\mathbb Z$ be the unipotent limit of
> $\mathfrak B^{\mathrm{cont}}_{j!}$.  In $D(\mathrm{Solid}_{\mathbb Z})$,
> $$D\epsilon\simeq\mathbb Q[-1].$$
> Hence the dual unipotent of the all-prime Borel $j_!$ class is a shifted
> boundary object, not a degree-$0$ group.
>
> **Theorem 94b (finite signed shadows survive).** For every finite support
> $S$, if $d_S:\mathbb Z^S\to\mathbb Z^{|S|-1}$ is the recollement boundary,
> then finite Verdier duality sends
> $$d_S\longmapsto-d_S^T,\qquad D^2(d_S)=d_S.$$
> The sign is visible over $\mathbb Z$ and collapses modulo $2$.
>
> **Theorem 94c (boundary functional-equation shadow).** The Pass-65/77
> antipode sign survives all-prime as the biduality sign
> $$\eta_\epsilon=-\mathrm{id}_\epsilon.$$
> This is a functional-equation shadow only after replacing the Weyl operator
> by the degree-$1$ finite-adele boundary
> $0\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb A_f\to\epsilon\to0$.
>
> **Theorem 94d (no forbidden Weyl flip).** Since
> $$\operatorname{Hom}^0_{\mathrm{Solid}}(\epsilon,\mathbb Q)=0,$$
> the duality does not create an opposite unipotent, a standard intertwiner,
> or a degree-$0$ Weyl/Fourier flip.

### Pass 95 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Package the boundary-shadow functional equation as a constant-term or
two-term Borel complex natural under conductor restriction.

Proposer:
The right package is the two-term Borel constant-term complex
$$
C_B:=\mathbb Q^\times\ltimes[\mathbb Q\to\mathbb A_f],
$$
in cohomological degrees $0\to1$.  Its unipotent boundary is exactly the
finite-adele row already isolated in Passes 84--86 and 94:
$$
0\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb A_f\to
\epsilon=\widehat{\mathbb Z}/\mathbb Z\to0.
$$
Thus
$$
H^0(C_B)=0,\qquad H^1(C_B)=\mathbb A_f/\mathbb Q\cong\epsilon.
$$
The global Levi $\mathbb Q^\times$ acts by scalar multiplication on the
two-term complex.  This is the constant-term form of the functional-equation
shadow: it keeps the boundary and the antipode sign, but it does not introduce
an opposite Borel.

The finite conductor shadow explains why this class is invisible to ordinary
finite quotients.  At conductor $N$ the complex is
$$
C_{B,N}=(\mathbb Z/N)^\times\ltimes
\left[\mathbb Z/N\to\prod_{p^e\parallel N}\mathbb Z/p^e\right].
$$
The diagonal map is an isomorphism by CRT, so $H^0(C_{B,N})=H^1(C_{B,N})=0$.
The boundary appears only after taking the all-prime solid/pro limit, not at a
fixed conductor.

Skeptic:
There are two traps.  First, finite CRT lifts can imitate support
zero-insertion at each conductor, but this is not an exact all-prime map:
the idempotent vector $(1\text{ on }S,0\text{ on }T\setminus S)$ is not a
diagonal integer in $\prod_{p\in T}\mathbb Z_p$.  Hence support enlargement
remains a span or a choice, not a canonical morphism.  Second, calling
$C_B$ a functional equation is safe only if "functional equation" means
"constant-term boundary identity."  It is not a standard intertwiner,
because the Pass-81 wall
$$
\operatorname{Hom}^0_{\mathrm{Solid}}(\epsilon,\mathbb Q)=0
$$
still forbids a Weyl/Fourier operator.

Formalist:
> **Theorem 95a (constant-term Borel complex).** Define
> $$C_B=\mathbb Q^\times\ltimes[\mathbb Q\to\mathbb A_f].$$
> Then in the solid boundary sense
> $$H^0(C_B)=0,\qquad H^1(C_B)=\mathbb A_f/\mathbb Q
> \cong\widehat{\mathbb Z}/\mathbb Z=\epsilon.$$
>
> **Theorem 95b (finite conductor acyclicity).** For every finite conductor
> $N$,
> $$\mathbb Z/N\to\prod_{p^e\parallel N}\mathbb Z/p^e$$
> is an isomorphism by CRT.  Hence every fixed finite conductor shadow of
> $C_B$ is ordinary-acyclic.
>
> **Theorem 95c (naturality and support direction).** If $N\mid M$, conductor
> reduction gives a commuting square of two-term complexes and preserves the
> Borel unit class.  For finite supports $S\subseteq T$, projection
> $T\to S$ is canonical, while exact zero-insertion $S\to T$ is not an
> all-prime diagonal-preserving map; it is only a finite-conductor CRT choice.
>
> **Theorem 95d (functional equation without Weyl operator).** The complex
> $C_B$ is the constant-term functional-equation shadow of the all-prime
> Borel class.  It has no nontrivial Whittaker component and no standard
> Weyl/Fourier intertwiner.

identify the exact data lost by passing from global to local Levi/stalk data.

Proposer:
For a finite prime support $S$, the comparison should be made before
rationalizing all the way to the full finite-adele row.  The compact
finite-support skeleton of Pass 95 is
$$
C_B^{\mathrm{int}}(S)
=\mathbb Q^\times\ltimes
\left[\mathbb Z\to\prod_{p\in S}\mathbb Z_p\right],
$$
where $\mathbb Z$ maps diagonally.  The local Loeb sheafification is
$$
C_L(S)=(\mathbb Q^\times)^S\ltimes
\left[\mathbb Z^S\to\prod_{p\in S}\mathbb Z_p\right],
$$
where $\mathbb Z^S$ maps coordinatewise.  There is a canonical map of
two-term complexes
$$
\alpha_S:C_B^{\mathrm{int}}(S)\longrightarrow C_L(S)
$$
given by diagonal Levi
$\mathbb Q^\times\to(\mathbb Q^\times)^S$, diagonal degree-$0$ unipotent
$\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z^S$, and the identity on
$\prod_{p\in S}\mathbb Z_p$.

On unipotent $H^1$, this is exactly the old Loeb/Rosser descent map:
$$
(\prod_{p\in S}\mathbb Z_p)/\Delta\mathbb Z
\longrightarrow
\prod_{p\in S}(\mathbb Z_p/\mathbb Z).
$$
Its kernel is
$$
K_S=\mathbb Z^S/\Delta\mathbb Z\cong\mathbb Z^{|S|-1}.
$$
Thus the kernel lost by local Loebification is not vague: it is the
horizontal Rosser kernel from Passes 61, 91, and 92, now presented as the
degree-$0$ quotient of a map of two-term constant-term complexes.

map
$$
\mathbb Q^\times\to(\mathbb Q^\times)^S

is diagonal and injective.  Local Loebification does not quotient out a
Levi kernel; it adds independent local Levi choices.  The measuring object is
therefore the quotient
$$
\Lambda_S=(\mathbb Q^\times)^S/\Delta\mathbb Q^\times,
$$
or, in a finite proxy $G$ for the Levi, a quotient of size $|G|^{|S|-1}$.
So the comparison has two components:
$$
K_S=\mathbb Z^S/\Delta\mathbb Z
\quad\text{on the unipotent boundary,}
$$
and
$$
\Lambda_S=(\mathbb Q^\times)^S/\Delta\mathbb Q^\times
\quad\text{on Levi coherence.}
$$
Only the first is literally the kernel of the $H^1$ map.

### Pass 99 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Construct the exact bridge from finite-support torsion boundaries to the
all-prime constant-term complex, and decide whether the support-limit collapse
is canonical.

Proposer:
The finite-support triangle is already present in Passes 97--98:
$$
K_{\mathbb Z,S}\to K_{\mathbb Q,S}\to T_S\to K_{\mathbb Z,S}[1],
$$
where
$$
K_{\mathbb Z,S}=\mathbb Z^S/\Delta\mathbb Z,\qquad
K_{\mathbb Q,S}=\mathbb Q^S/\Delta\mathbb Q,\qquad
T_S=(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)^S/\Delta(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z).
$$
To map this triangle to the single constant-term generator, choose a primitive
zero-sum functional
$$
c=(c_p)_{p\in S}\in\mathbb Z^S,\qquad \sum_{p\in S}c_p=0,\qquad
\gcd_{p\in S}(c_p)=1.
$$
Then $c$ descends to maps
$$
K_{\mathbb Z,S}\to\mathbb Z,\qquad
K_{\mathbb Q,S}\to\mathbb Q,\qquad
T_S\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z,
$$
and these maps form a morphism of exact triangles to
$$
\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z[1].
$$
Composing with the all-prime finite-adele realization gives the
constant-term row $[\mathbb Q\to\mathbb A_f]$ with boundary
$\epsilon=\mathbb A_f/\mathbb Q$.

Skeptic:
There is no canonical collapse $T_S\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ without choosing
$c$.  A map out of $T_S$ is represented by a zero-sum integral functional on
$S$; the only support-symmetric such functional is $0$.  Thus the operation
which collapses $|S|-1$ finite coordinates to one generator is not a plain
support limit.  It is a torsor of primitive boundary orientations.  The exact
bridge exists after a choice, but the choice must be tracked rather than
silently erased.

Formalist:
For $r=|S|-1$ and primitive $c$, the induced map on $N$-torsion is
surjective:
$$
T_S[N]\twoheadrightarrow(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)[N].
$$
Since $|T_S[N]|=N^r$ and $|(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)[N]|=N$, its kernel has size
$$
N^{r-1}=N^{|S|-2}
$$
when $|S|\ge2$.  The antipode acts by $c\mapsto -c$, so it negates the
boundary class.  This sign is visible over $\mathbb Z$ and collapses modulo
$2$, matching the Pass-94 finite signed-dual behavior.  The target remains
shifted through $D\epsilon\simeq\mathbb Q[-1]$, so the construction still
does not produce a degree-$0$ Weyl/Fourier map $\epsilon\to\mathbb Q$.

> **Theorem 99a (finite exact triangle).** The inclusion
> $K_{\mathbb Z,S}\hookrightarrow K_{\mathbb Q,S}$ gives the exact triangle
> $$K_{\mathbb Z,S}\to K_{\mathbb Q,S}\to T_S\to K_{\mathbb Z,S}[1].$$
>
> **Theorem 99b (collapse parameter).** A morphism from this triangle to
> $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is determined by an integral
> zero-sum functional $c\in\mathbb Z^S$; it is surjective on the
> $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ term precisely when $c$ is primitive.
>
> **Theorem 99c (noncanonical support collapse).** No support-symmetric
> nonzero primitive $c$ exists.  Therefore the collapse of $T_S$ to one
> constant-term generator is not canonical; it is an orientation choice.
>
> **Theorem 99d (antipode/no-Weyl compatibility).** The antipode sends
> $c$ to $-c$, negating the boundary class, and the resulting bridge to
> $[\mathbb Q\to\mathbb A_f]$ remains shifted; no degree-$0$ Weyl map
> $\epsilon\to\mathbb Q$ is created.

### Pass 100 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Study the orientation torsor of primitive zero-sum boundary functionals under
support change.

Proposer:
For each finite support $S$ with $|S|\ge2$, define
$$
\mathcal O_S=\{c=(c_p)_{p\in S}\in\mathbb Z^S:
\sum_{p\in S}c_p=0,\ \gcd_{p\in S}(c_p)=1\}.
$$
This is the set of primitive collapses
$$
T_S=(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)^S/\Delta(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)
\twoheadrightarrow \mathbb Q/\mathbb Z.
$$
For an inclusion $S\subseteq T$, the canonical operation is not restriction
but pullback along the boundary projection $T_T\to T_S$.  On functionals it is
extension by zero:
$$
e_{S,T}(c)_p=
\begin{cases}
c_p,&p\in S,\\
0,&p\in T\setminus S.
\end{cases}
$$
This preserves the zero-sum condition, primitivity, and the induced collapse.
It is strictly functorial:
$$
e_{T,U}\circ e_{S,T}=e_{S,U}.
$$

Skeptic:
The reverse direction fails.  If $d\in\mathcal O_T$, its restriction to
$S$ need not sum to zero, so it may not define any collapse on $T_S$.  Example:
for $S=\{2,3\}$ and $T=\{2,3,5\}$,
$$
d=(1,1,-2)\in\mathcal O_T
$$
restricts to $(1,1)$ on $S$, whose sum is $2$.  Thus there is no canonical
projection $\mathcal O_T\to\mathcal O_S$.  Also, no support-symmetric
primitive orientation exists: a symmetric integral functional is constant,
and zero-sum forces it to be $0$.

Formalist:
For zero-extended orientations, finite kernels factor exactly.  If
$r_S=|S|-1$ and $r_T=|T|-1$, then the primitive collapse on $T_S$ has
$N$-torsion kernel of size $N^{r_S-1}$; after extension to $T$, the kernel has
size
$$
N^{r_T-1}=N^{r_S-1}\cdot N^{|T|-|S|}.
$$
The second factor is precisely the new support kernel introduced by
$T_T\to T_S$.  The antipode action is compatible with support pullback:
$$
e_{S,T}(-c)=-e_{S,T}(c).
$$
Hence the natural finite object is not a single chosen collapse but the
oriented-support groupoid/stack whose objects are pairs $(S,c)$ and whose
morphisms are generated by zero-extension and the antipode.

> **Theorem 100a (orientation objects).** For $|S|\ge2$, primitive collapses
> $T_S\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ are represented by
> $\mathcal O_S=\{c\in\mathbb Z^S:\sum c_p=0,\gcd(c_p)=1\}$, with free
> antipode action $c\mapsto -c$.
>
> **Theorem 100b (zero-extension functoriality).** For $S\subseteq T$,
> $e_{S,T}:\mathcal O_S\to\mathcal O_T$ given by zero-extension preserves
> primitivity, collapse compatibility, and antipode sign, and is strictly
> functorial along support chains.
>
> **Theorem 100c (no projection of orientations).** There is no canonical
> projection $\mathcal O_T\to\mathcal O_S$: restriction can fail the zero-sum
> descent condition.
>
> **Theorem 100d (no symmetric all-prime orientation).** The only
> support-symmetric zero-sum functional is $0$, so the all-prime
> constant-term generator is obtained only after choosing, quotienting, or
> forgetting the orientation torsor.

### Pass 101 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Package the oriented-support groupoid/stack and compare the antipode quotient
with the Pass-94 functional-equation sign.

Proposer:
For each finite support $S$ with $|S|\ge2$, keep
$$
\mathcal O_S=\{c\in\mathbb Z^S:\sum_{p\in S}c_p=0,\ \gcd(c_p)=1\}.
$$
Define the **signed oriented-support action groupoid** by taking objects
$(S,c)$ with $c\in\mathcal O_S$.  A morphism
$$
(S,c)\longrightarrow (T,d)
$$
is an inclusion $S\subseteq T$ together with a sign
$\sigma\in\{\pm1\}$ such that
$$
d=\sigma e_{S,T}(c),
$$
where $e_{S,T}$ is zero-extension.  Identities have sign $+1$, and
composition multiplies signs:
$$
(\tau,U)\circ(\sigma,T)=(\tau\sigma,U).
$$
The antipode is the sign $-1$ morphism
$(S,c)\to(S,-c)$ over the same support; it squares to the identity.

Skeptic:
The coarse antipode quotient
$$
[c]=\{c,-c\}
$$
does identify the two orientations of a primitive collapse line and therefore
presents the single all-prime generator more economically.  But this quotient
has no memory of whether a path used the sign $+1$ or $-1$.  Thus the plain
coarse quotient is too coarse for the Pass-94 functional-equation sign: it
remembers a primitive line, not the signed transport along that line.

Formalist:
The right package is either the signed action groupoid itself or the coarse
quotient equipped with its residual $\mathbb Z/2$ sign local system.  The
local system records the sign character of the double cover
$(S,c)\to(S,[c])$.  It keeps exactly the data needed for the Pass-94 rule that
the antipode negates the boundary class.  At finite level $N$, multiplication
by $-1$ on $(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)[N]$ is visible for $N>2$ and collapses when
$N=2$, matching the earlier mod-$2$ sign collapse.  No degree-$0$ Weyl map
$\epsilon\to\mathbb Q$ is produced; the construction only packages the sign
of the shifted boundary generator.

> **Theorem 101a (signed support category).** The data above form a strict
> support category/action groupoid: zero-extension supplies the support
> transition and signs compose multiplicatively.
>
> **Theorem 101b (antipode action).** The antipode is the sign $-1$ morphism
> $(S,c)\to(S,-c)$ and is involutive.  It is compatible with all
> zero-extension morphisms.
>
> **Theorem 101c (coarse quotient loses sign).** The quotient
> $[c]=\{c,-c\}$ presents primitive collapse lines but forgets the path sign;
> therefore it is insufficient by itself for the Pass-94 signed-duality
> bookkeeping.
>
> **Theorem 101d (sign local system).** The signed action groupoid, or the
> coarse quotient plus its $\mathbb Z/2$ sign local system, preserves exactly
> the antipode sign visible on finite $N$-torsion for $N>2$ and invisible at
> $N=2$.

The plain antipode quotient $[c]=\{c,-c\}$ still cannot remember this action.
After quotienting, the primitive line remains, but the distinction between
$+\delta_\epsilon$ and $-\delta_\epsilon$ is absent.  Conversely, adding more
finite conductor data is unnecessary: at finite level $N$, the class is just
the signed Bockstein generator
$$
\pm1\in\mathbb Z/N,
$$
so the only collapse is the expected one, $1=-1$ when $N=2$.

Formalist:
The exact boundary/Yoneda class representing the shifted bidual object is
the boundary morphism
$$
\partial_\epsilon:\epsilon\to\mathbb Q[1]
$$
associated to $0\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb A_f\to\epsilon\to0$.  Under the
identification
$$
D\epsilon\simeq\mathbb Q[-1],
$$
this same class is the shifted generator.  A one-sided sign change on the
quotient or kernel multiplies the extension class by $-1$; applying the sign
on both sides multiplies by $(-1)^2=1$, so the biduality square is compatible
with the involutive antipode.  This still does not provide a degree-$0$
Weyl/Fourier morphism $\epsilon\to\mathbb Q$.

> **Theorem 102a (signed boundary action).** The $\mathbb Z/2$ local system
> acts on the unit extension and the all-prime finite-adele row by
> $\beta\mapsto\sigma\beta$ and
> $\delta_\epsilon\mapsto\sigma\delta_\epsilon$.
>
> **Theorem 102b (finite Bockstein shadow).** At finite level $N$, the signed
> boundary class is $\sigma\in\mathbb Z/N$.  The sign is visible exactly when
> $N>2$ and collapses when $N=2$.
>
> **Theorem 102c (biduality sign).** The shifted class
> $D\epsilon\simeq\mathbb Q[-1]$ carries the same one-sided sign.  Acting on
> both source and target squares the sign to $+1$.
>
> **Theorem 102d (no extra Weyl data).** The local system is sufficient for
> the finite sign bookkeeping and does not create a degree-$0$ map
> $\epsilon\to\mathbb Q$.

### Pass 103 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Package the signed boundary class as a natural system over finite conductor
reductions and compare it with the Pass-95 CRT-acyclic constant-term
complexes.

Proposer:
For every conductor $N$, write the signed finite Bockstein class as
$$
b_N^\sigma=\sigma\in\mathbb Z/N,\qquad \sigma\in\{\pm1\}.
$$
If $M\mid N$, conductor reduction
$$
\rho_{N,M}:\mathbb Z/N\to\mathbb Z/M
$$
satisfies
$$
\rho_{N,M}(b_N^\sigma)=b_M^\sigma.
$$
Thus the Pass-102 sign local system is a natural transformation over the
finite conductor category.  The finite sign can disappear only when the
target modulus is $2$, where $1=-1$.

Skeptic:
This naturality should not be mistaken for a new finite obstruction.  The
Pass-95 finite conductor complex was
$$
C_{B,N}=(\mathbb Z/N)^\times\ltimes
\left[\mathbb Z/N\to\prod_{p^e\parallel N}\mathbb Z/p^e\right],
$$
with diagonal map an isomorphism by CRT.  Twisting the diagonal by
$\sigma=\pm1$ gives
$$
d_N^\sigma(x)=(\sigma x\bmod p^e)_{p^e\parallel N}.
$$
Since $\sigma$ is a unit, $d_N^\sigma$ is still a CRT isomorphism.  Hence
the signed finite shadows remain ordinary-acyclic.

Formalist:
For $M\mid N$, the square comparing $d_N^\sigma$ with $d_M^\sigma$ commutes:
reduce first and then apply the signed diagonal, or apply the signed diagonal
and reduce each prime-power coordinate.  Therefore the signed boundary class
is functorial over conductor reductions and introduces no finite
sign-twisted cohomology.  The all-prime class still lives in the pro/solid
boundary; fixed finite CRT shadows see zero cohomology.  This also preserves
the Pass-95 caution: support projection is canonical, but support enlargement
remains only a finite CRT choice/span and not a canonical all-prime
diagonal-preserving map.

> **Theorem 103a (signed Bockstein naturality).** For every $M\mid N$,
> $\rho_{N,M}(\sigma\bmod N)=\sigma\bmod M$.
>
> **Theorem 103b (signed finite CRT acyclicity).** The signed differential
> $d_N^\sigma:\mathbb Z/N\to\prod_{p^e\parallel N}\mathbb Z/p^e$ is an
> isomorphism for $\sigma=\pm1$.  Thus fixed finite signed conductor shadows
> have $H^0=H^1=0$.
>
> **Theorem 103c (no new conductor obstruction).** Conductor reduction
> commutes with the signed CRT differentials.  The only finite sign collapse
> is reduction to modulus $2$.
>
> **Theorem 103d (support caution persists).** Signed conductor naturality
> does not make support enlargement a canonical all-prime map; it remains a
> finite-conductor choice/span.

### Pass 104 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Assemble the signed conductor system into a pro/solid all-prime boundary
object and decide where the orientation double cover lives.

Proposer:
Pass 103 gave a compatible finite conductor system
$$
b_N^\sigma=\sigma\bmod N,\qquad \sigma\in\{\pm1\}.
$$
Taking the inverse limit over conductors gives
$$
\{b_N^\sigma\}_N=\sigma\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}.
$$
Because $\sigma=\pm1$ is an ordinary diagonal integer, its image in
$$
\epsilon=\widehat{\mathbb Z}/\mathbb Z
$$
is zero.  Hence the sign does not produce two distinct points of the
all-prime boundary object $\epsilon$.

Skeptic:
This is the key correction to a tempting but false picture: the finite signs
are visible in $\mathbb Z/N$ for $N>2$, but the compatible pro-system they
define is still an integral point of $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$.  Once we quotient
by $\mathbb Z$ to form $\epsilon$, both $+1$ and $-1$ vanish as points.  Thus
there is no genuine two-sheeted cover of $\epsilon$ whose fibers are the two
primitive orientations.

Formalist:
The sign survives as monodromy of the boundary line, not as an
$\epsilon$-point.  The boundary/Yoneda class
$$
\delta_\epsilon=[0\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb A_f\to\epsilon\to0]
$$
spans the shifted line
$$
D\epsilon\simeq\mathbb Q[-1].
$$
The local system acts by
$$
\delta_\epsilon\mapsto\sigma\delta_\epsilon.
$$
Therefore the minimal categorical package is:

1. the oriented-support action groupoid $(S,c)$ with zero-extension;
2. the finite-conductor pro-system of CRT-isomorphism complexes
   $C^\sigma_{B,N}$;
3. a $B\mathbb Z/2$ local system on the boundary/Yoneda line.

This package carries support, conductor, and sign while preserving
$$
\operatorname{Hom}^0(\epsilon,\mathbb Q)=0.
$$

> **Theorem 104a (pro-sign limit).** The compatible system
> $\{\sigma\bmod N\}_N$ has inverse limit $\sigma\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}$.
>
> **Theorem 104b (epsilon-point absorption).** Since $\sigma=\pm1$ is a
> diagonal integer, its image in $\epsilon=\widehat{\mathbb Z}/\mathbb Z$ is
> zero.  The two signs do not define distinct points of $\epsilon$.
>
> **Theorem 104c (local-system survival).** The sign survives as the
> $\mathbb Z/2$ action on the boundary/Yoneda class
> $\delta_\epsilon$, equivalently on $D\epsilon\simeq\mathbb Q[-1]$.
>
> **Theorem 104d (minimal no-Weyl package).** The minimal package is the
> oriented-support groupoid over the finite-conductor pro-system with a
> $B\mathbb Z/2$ boundary-line local system.  It does not create a degree-$0$
> Weyl map $\epsilon\to\mathbb Q$.

### Pass 105 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Compare the signed pro-boundary package with support projections and
zero-extension spans, and isolate the exact descent/colimit statement for
all-prime primitive orientations.

Proposer:
For finite support $S$, keep
$$
\mathcal O_S=
\{c=(c_p)_{p\in S}\in\mathbb Z^S:
\sum_{p\in S}c_p=0,\ \gcd(c_p)=1\}.
$$
If $S\subseteq T$, the canonical orientation map is zero-extension
$$
e_{S,T}:\mathcal O_S\to\mathcal O_T,\qquad
(e_{S,T}c)_p=
\begin{cases}
c_p,&p\in S,\\
0,&p\in T\setminus S.
\end{cases}
$$
This preserves zero-sum, primitivity, and the antipode
$c\mapsto -c$, and it composes strictly:
$$
e_{T,U}e_{S,T}=e_{S,U}.
$$
Thus finite oriented supports form a filtered colimit by zero-padding.

Skeptic:
This colimit should not be called descent for a sheaf of orientations on the
support poset.  The boundary groups have canonical support projection
$$
T_T\to T_S,
$$
but primitive orientations do not have a total restriction map in the
opposite direction.  The obstruction is already visible at three primes:
$$
(1,1,-2)\in\mathcal O_{\{2,3,5\}}
$$
restricts to $(1,1)$ on $\{2,3\}$, and this has sum $2$, not $0$.  Therefore
the all-prime package cannot be a plain sheaf with maps
$\mathcal O_T\to\mathcal O_S$ unless one discards genuine orientations or
adds noncanonical correction terms.

Formalist:
The correct object is the Grothendieck/span presentation over finite
supports:

1. forward leg on orientation torsors: $e_{S,T}:\mathcal O_S\to\mathcal O_T$;
2. backward leg on boundary groups: $T_T\to T_S$;
3. sign line: the $B\mathbb Z/2$ local system acting on
   $\delta_\epsilon$.

The colimit identifies $(S,c)$ with $(T,e_{S,T}c)$, equivalently it presents
primitive finitely supported zero-sum integer functionals on the set of all
primes, modulo padded zeros.  A support-symmetric all-prime orientation is
still impossible: a constant finitely supported functional is zero-sum only
when it is zero, hence it is not primitive.  Passing to the antipode quotient
gives primitive lines $[c]=\{c,-c\}$, but the sign must remain as the
boundary-line local system.

> **Theorem 105a (zero-extension colimit).** The assignment
> $S\mapsto\mathcal O_S$ is covariant for support inclusions by
> zero-extension, and these maps form a filtered colimit of primitive
> finitely supported zero-sum orientations.
>
> **Theorem 105b (restriction obstruction).** There is no canonical total
> restriction map $\mathcal O_T\to\mathcal O_S$ for $S\subseteq T$, since
> deleting coordinates can destroy zero-sum.
>
> **Theorem 105c (span-stack presentation).** The support-descent package is
> a span/Grothendieck object combining orientation zero-extension,
> boundary-group projection, and the $B\mathbb Z/2$ boundary-line local
> system.  It is not a plain sheaf of primitive orientations on the support
> poset.
>
> **Theorem 105d (no symmetric all-prime orientation).** No nonzero
> support-symmetric primitive all-prime orientation exists.  The all-prime
> generator is obtained only by choosing a primitive orientation line,
> quotienting by the antipode, or forgetting orientation data, with the sign
> retained on the boundary line.

### Pass 106 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Compute the obstruction to stackifying primitive orientations over finite
supports with restriction maps, and state the universal property of the
span-stack/left-Kan colimit package.

Proposer:
The obstruction is already visible before any higher stack language is
needed.  For $S\subseteq T$ and $d\in\mathcal O_T$, coordinate deletion gives
a vector $d|_S\in\mathbb Z^S$ whose additive defect is
$$
\Delta_{T,S}(d)=\sum_{p\in S}d_p.
$$
Since $d$ is zero-sum on $T$,
$$
\Delta_{T,S}(d)=-\sum_{p\in T\setminus S}d_p.
$$
Thus naive restriction lands in $\mathcal O_S$ only if
$$
\Delta_{T,S}(d)=0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\gcd_{p\in S}(d_p)=1.
$$
The second condition is independent: the vector
$$
(2,-2,1,-1)\in\mathcal O_{\{2,3,5,7\}}
$$
has zero additive defect on $\{2,3\}$, but restricts to $(2,-2)$, which is
not primitive.

Skeptic:
One might try to repair a nonzero defect by subtracting it from one chosen
coordinate, but this is exactly the missing choice.  A repair is a section of
the summation map
$$
\Sigma_S:\mathbb Z^S\to\mathbb Z,\qquad
(a_p)\mapsto\sum_{p\in S}a_p.
$$
Choosing the first prime, last prime, or any preferred basepoint gives
different repaired orientations.  These can even represent different
antipode-quotient lines, so the ambiguity is not just the existing
$\mathbb Z/2$ sign.

Formalist:
No support-symmetric integral section of $\Sigma_S$ exists for $|S|>1$.  If
such a section were symmetric, the image of $1\in\mathbb Z$ would be a
constant vector $(k,\dots,k)$, forcing
$$
|S|k=1,
$$
which has no integer solution.  Therefore a restriction sheaf can be made
only after adding extra structure, such as a basepoint or ordering.  The
forgetful passage back to unbased finite supports loses naturality.

The universal property should therefore be stated covariantly.  Let
$$
\mathcal O_{\mathbb P}^{\mathrm{fin}}
=\operatorname*{colim}_{S\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{fin}}(\mathbb P)}
\mathcal O_S
$$
under zero-extension.  A family of maps
$F_S:\mathcal O_S\to X$ factors uniquely through
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb P}^{\mathrm{fin}}$ exactly when
$$
F_T(e_{S,T}c)=F_S(c)
$$
for every $S\subseteq T$.  The colimit representative is obtained by
trimming padded zero coordinates.  The antipode quotient
$[c]=\{c,-c\}$ is the coarse orientation line, while the distinction between
$+\delta_\epsilon$ and $-\delta_\epsilon$ remains the $B\mathbb Z/2$
boundary-line local system.

> **Theorem 106a (restriction defect).** Coordinate deletion
> $d\mapsto d|_S$ has obstruction
> $\Delta_{T,S}(d)=\sum_{p\in S}d_p$.  It defines a primitive restriction
> only on the partial domain where $\Delta_{T,S}(d)=0$ and primitivity
> survives.
>
> **Theorem 106b (no symmetric repair).** Repairing nonzero defect requires a
> section of $\Sigma_S:\mathbb Z^S\to\mathbb Z$.  No support-symmetric
> integer section exists for $|S|>1$.
>
> **Theorem 106c (universal colimit).** The all-prime primitive-orientation
> object has the left-Kan/filtered-colimit universal property for
> zero-extension-compatible families.  It is primitive finitely supported
> zero-sum functions modulo padded zeros.
>
> **Theorem 106d (quotient plus local system).** The antipode quotient gives
> orientation lines, but the functional-equation sign remains as the
> $B\mathbb Z/2$ local system on the boundary/Yoneda line; no degree-$0$
> Weyl map is created.

### Pass 107 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Model correction choices as torsors under $\ker\Sigma_S$ and decide whether
the support-defect cocycle is Rosser/cosheaf-like or only an ordinary choice
obstruction.

Proposer:
For a finite support $S$, define
$$
K_S=\ker\Sigma_S
=\{a\in\mathbb Z^S:\sum_{p\in S}a_p=0\}.
$$
Given $S\subseteq T$ and $d\in\mathcal O_T$, coordinate deletion gives
$u=d|_S\in\mathbb Z^S$ with defect $\Delta=\Sigma_S(u)$.  An additive repair
is a vector
$$
r=u-a,\qquad \Sigma_S(a)=\Delta,
$$
so that $\Sigma_S(r)=0$.  If $r$ and $r'$ are two additive repairs, then
$$
r'-r\in K_S,
$$
and conversely $r+k$ is an additive repair for every $k\in K_S$.  Thus
additive repairs form a $K_S$-torsor.

Skeptic:
The word "repair" hides a primitivity trap.  The additive repair torsor is
larger than the primitive repair locus.  For instance, in support $\{2,3\}$,
the vector $(1,-1)$ is primitive, and $(1,-1)\in K_S$; adding it again gives
$$(2,-2),$$
which is zero-sum but not primitive.  Therefore primitive repairs are not a
torsor under the full $K_S$.  They are the primitive locus inside the
additive torsor.

Formalist:
Choosing a basepoint $b\in S$ gives a section
$$
s_b:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z^S,\qquad
s_b(n)=n e_b.
$$
The transition between two basepoints is
$$
\tau_{a,b}=s_b(1)-s_a(1)\in K_S,
$$
and
$$
\tau_{a,b}+\tau_{b,c}=\tau_{a,c}.
$$
Thus these transitions are coboundaries of chosen splittings.  Along an
inclusion $S\subseteq T$, basepointed splittings are natural exactly when
the basepoint is preserved; changing the basepoint produces a $K_T$-valued
transition.

This differs from the Rosser/cosheaf phantom: at each finite support we have
a split short exact sequence
$$
0\to K_S\to\mathbb Z^S\xrightarrow{\Sigma_S}\mathbb Z\to0
$$
after choosing any basepoint.  There is no non-Mittag-Leffler inverse tower
or unavoidable derived limit.  The noncanonicity is an ordinary choice
torsor, not a persistent $\varprojlim^1$ class.  Linear sections also commute
with the antipode:
$$
\operatorname{repair}_{s_b}(-d)=-\operatorname{repair}_{s_b}(d),
$$
so the $B\mathbb Z/2$ boundary-line local system survives unchanged.

> **Theorem 107a (additive repair torsor).** For fixed deletion data, the
> additive repairs form a free transitive $K_S=\ker\Sigma_S$ torsor.
>
> **Theorem 107b (primitive locus refinement).** The primitive repair choices
> are not stable under all of $K_S$; they form a primitive locus inside the
> additive torsor.
>
> **Theorem 107c (basepoint coboundaries).** Basepointed splittings
> $s_b$ trivialize the additive repair torsor, and transition functions
> $s_b-s_a$ are $K_S$-valued coboundaries satisfying the cocycle identity.
>
> **Theorem 107d (ordinary choice, not phantom).** The support-defect repair
> data is finite-level split choice data, not a Rosser/cosheaf phantom
> $\varprojlim^1$ class.  Antipode compatibility and the $B\mathbb Z/2$
> boundary local system are preserved.

`artifacts/reports/pass107-correction-torsors-support-defect-check.json`,
PASS): the checker verifies additive repair torsors under $K_S$, the
non-stability of the primitive locus under the full kernel, basepoint
transition coboundaries and their cocycle identity, inclusion naturality only
when the basepoint is preserved, antipode compatibility of linear repairs,
and the verdict that the data is ordinary split choice rather than a
Rosser/cosheaf phantom.

### Pass 108 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Classify the integral equivariant obstruction for support-symmetric repair
sections and compare it with the antipode local system.

Proposer:
Let $S$ be a finite support of size $n>1$.  The symmetric group
$G=\operatorname{Sym}(S)$ acts on $\mathbb Z^S$ by permuting coordinates, and
the summation map
$$
\Sigma_S:\mathbb Z^S\to\mathbb Z
$$
is $G$-equivariant when $\mathbb Z$ has the trivial action.  A
support-symmetric integral section is therefore an invariant vector
$v\in(\mathbb Z^S)^G$ with $\Sigma_S(v)=1$.  But
$$
(\mathbb Z^S)^G=\mathbb Z\mathbf 1_S,
\qquad
\mathbf 1_S=(1,\dots,1),
$$
and
$$
\Sigma_S(k\mathbf 1_S)=nk.
$$
So the invariant image is $n\mathbb Z$, and no integral equivariant section
exists for $n>1$.

Skeptic:
This does not mean the exact sequence is unsplittable after changing
coefficients.  Over $\mathbb Q$, there is a canonical symmetric barycentric
section
$$
s_{\mathrm{bar}}(1)=\frac1n\mathbf 1_S.
$$
Thus the obstruction is not a mysterious phantom.  It is exactly the
denominator $n$: an equivariant integral lift of an integer $m$ exists iff
$$
n\mid m.
$$
Basepoint splittings $s_b(1)=e_b$ are integral but not support-symmetric;
the barycentric splitting is support-symmetric but rational.

Formalist:
In the augmentation sequence of $G$-modules
$$
0\to K_S\to\mathbb Z^S\xrightarrow{\Sigma_S}\mathbb Z\to0,
$$
the obstruction to an integral $G$-equivariant splitting is the quotient
$$
\mathbb Z/\Sigma_S((\mathbb Z^S)^G)
=\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z.
$$
After inverting $n$, or after tensoring with $\mathbb Q$, this obstruction
vanishes.  Under support inclusions, barycentric splittings are not natural:
extending the $S$-barycenter by zero differs from the $T$-barycenter by a
vector in $\ker(\Sigma_T)\otimes\mathbb Q$.  This gives a rational transition
class to study next.

The antipode is independent of this denominator obstruction.  It acts by the
scalar sign on the boundary/Yoneda line and commutes with all support
permutations.  Replacing $1$ by $-1$ changes the barycenter to
$-\frac1n\mathbf 1_S$ but does not change the denominator.  Hence the
$B\mathbb Z/2$ local system remains separate from the integral
support-symmetry obstruction.

> **Theorem 108a (integral equivariant obstruction).** For $|S|=n>1$, the
> summation map $\Sigma_S:\mathbb Z^S\to\mathbb Z$ has no
> $\operatorname{Sym}(S)$-equivariant integral section.
>
> **Theorem 108b (barycentric rational section).** Over $\mathbb Q$, the
> barycentric vector $\frac1n\mathbf 1_S$ gives a canonical
> support-symmetric section.
>
> **Theorem 108c (exact denominator).** An equivariant integral lift of
> $m\in\mathbb Z$ exists iff $n\mid m$.  The obstruction is the finite
> denominator class $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$.
>
> **Theorem 108d (antipode independence).** The antipode local system acts on
> the boundary line and does not change the support-symmetry denominator
> obstruction.

Machine verification (`code/scripts/check-pass108.py` ->
`artifacts/reports/pass108-integral-equivariant-repair-section-check.json`,
PASS): the checker verifies that invariant integral vectors map to
$n\mathbb Z$, that the rational barycenter splits $\Sigma_S$ over
$\mathbb Q$, that integral equivariant lifts of $m$ exist exactly when
$n\mid m$, that barycentric sections are not natural under support inclusions
but differ by rational-kernel transitions, and that the antipode sign leaves
the denominator unchanged.

finite conductor/CRT denominator bookkeeping already present in the boundary

### Pass 109 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Compute barycentric transition denominators under support inclusions and
compare them with finite conductor/CRT bookkeeping.

Proposer:
For an inclusion of finite supports $S\subset T$, put $|S|=n$ and
$|T|=m$.  The rational barycentric sections are
$$
s_{\mathrm{bar},S}(1)=\frac1n\mathbf 1_S,\qquad
s_{\mathrm{bar},T}(1)=\frac1m\mathbf 1_T.
$$
After zero-extending the first vector to $T$, the transition is
$$
\tau_{S,T}:=e_{S,T}s_{\mathrm{bar},S}(1)-s_{\mathrm{bar},T}(1).
$$
Thus
$$
(\tau_{S,T})_p=
\begin{cases}
\frac1n-\frac1m=\frac{m-n}{nm}, & p\in S,\\[2mm]
-\frac1m, & p\in T\setminus S.
\end{cases}
$$
The sum is
$$
n\frac{m-n}{nm}+(m-n)\left(-\frac1m\right)=0,
$$
so $\tau_{S,T}\in K_T\otimes\mathbb Q$.

Skeptic:
This is a coboundary transition between rational splittings, so it should not
be promoted to a new Rosser or CRT phantom.  The correct invariant is the
denominator.  Let $g=\gcd(n,m)$, $n=ga$, and $m=gb$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$.
Any integer $D$ clearing the off-support entries must be divisible by $m$,
say $D=gbq$.  Clearing the on-support entries requires
$$
\frac{D(m-n)}{nm}
=\frac{q(b-a)}{a}\in\mathbb Z.
$$
Since $\gcd(a,b-a)=1$, this is equivalent to $a\mid q$.  Hence the minimal
clearing denominator is
$$
D=gab=\operatorname{lcm}(n,m).
$$
So a finite conductor $N$ clears this rational transition exactly when
$$
\operatorname{lcm}(n,m)\mid N.
$$

Formalist:
Clearing by $L=\operatorname{lcm}(n,m)=nm/g$ gives the integral vector
$$
\eta_{S,T}:=L\tau_{S,T}.
$$
Its entries are
$$
(\eta_{S,T})_p=
\begin{cases}
\frac{m-n}{g}, & p\in S,\\[2mm]
-\frac{n}{g}, & p\in T\setminus S.
\end{cases}
$$
This vector is zero-sum.  It is also primitive, because after writing
$n=ga$, $m=gb$, the two displayed integer values are $b-a$ and $-a$, and
$$
\gcd(b-a,a)=1.
$$
Thus barycentric transition denominators are not only obstruction data:
their minimal integral clearings produce canonical primitive zero-sum
vectors on the target support.

For a chain $S\subset T\subset U$, the rational transitions satisfy
$$
e_{T,U}\tau_{S,T}+\tau_{T,U}=\tau_{S,U}.
$$
This is simply the coboundary identity for the rational barycentric
splittings.  After choosing a common conductor that clears all three
transition denominators, the same identity holds integrally.  However, the
individually primitive clearings $\eta_{S,T}$, $\eta_{T,U}$, and
$\eta_{S,U}$ need not compose without rescaling; their coherence is a
separate conductor-cleared edge-data problem.

Comparison with the signed finite conductor package: at every finite
conductor $N$, the CRT map
$$
\mathbb Z/N\to\prod_{p^e\parallel N}\mathbb Z/p^e
$$
and its signed version remain isomorphisms.  Denominator clearance specifies
which conductors allow the rational support transition to be represented by
an integral zero-sum vector; it does not create finite CRT cohomology.  The
Pass-95/103 acyclicity statements therefore remain intact.

> $|T|=m$, the barycentric transition has values $(m-n)/(nm)$ on $S$ and
> $-1/m$ on $T\setminus S$, hence lies in $K_T\otimes\mathbb Q$.
>
> **Theorem 109b (exact denominator).** The exact denominator of
> $\tau_{S,T}$ is $\operatorname{lcm}(n,m)$.  A conductor $N$ clears
> $\tau_{S,T}$ iff $\operatorname{lcm}(n,m)\mid N$.
>
> **Theorem 109c (primitive cleared transition).** The minimally cleared
> vector $\eta_{S,T}=\operatorname{lcm}(n,m)\tau_{S,T}$ is an integral
> primitive zero-sum vector on $T$.
>
> **Theorem 109d (coboundary but not CRT cohomology).** The rational
> transitions satisfy the chain coboundary identity, while finite CRT and
> signed CRT conductor shadows remain bijective.  Thus the transition is
> normalized support-comparison data, not a new finite CRT cohomology class.

### Pass 110 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Determine the chain law for primitive conductor-cleared barycentric
transition vectors and compare it with primitive repair torsors.

Proposer:
Pass 109 attached to every support inclusion $S\subset T$ a rational
transition $\tau_{S,T}\in K_T\otimes\mathbb Q$ and its minimal integral
clearing
$$
\eta_{S,T}:=L_{S,T}\tau_{S,T},\qquad
L_{S,T}:=\operatorname{lcm}(|S|,|T|).
$$
If $|S|=n$, $|T|=m$, and $g=\gcd(n,m)$, then $\eta_{S,T}$ has entries
$(m-n)/g$ on $S$ and $-n/g$ on $T\setminus S$.  It is zero-sum and primitive.
So the apparent edge label is a primitive vector in $K_T$.

Skeptic:
The primitive label by itself is not functorial.  Along a chain
$S\subset T\subset U$, the rational transitions satisfy
$$
e_{T,U}\tau_{S,T}+\tau_{T,U}=\tau_{S,U}.
$$
But replacing each $\tau$ by its primitive clearing changes the denominators.
Let
$$
L_{S,T}=\operatorname{lcm}(|S|,|T|),\quad
L_{T,U}=\operatorname{lcm}(|T|,|U|),\quad
L_{S,U}=\operatorname{lcm}(|S|,|U|)
$$
and
$$
C=\operatorname{lcm}(L_{S,T},L_{T,U},L_{S,U}).
$$
Then the correct identity is weighted:
$$
\frac{C}{L_{S,T}}e_{T,U}\eta_{S,T}
+\frac{C}{L_{T,U}}\eta_{T,U}
=\frac{C}{L_{S,U}}\eta_{S,U}.
$$
Thus the primitive vector or primitive line alone loses necessary conductor
weights.  It is useful edge data, but only with its conductor attached.

Formalist:
The weighted chain law follows by multiplying the rational coboundary
identity by $C$.  Strict primitive composition
$$
e_{T,U}\eta_{S,T}+\eta_{T,U}=\eta_{S,U}
$$
can hold only when the denominator clearings agree in the relevant checked
chains:
$$
L_{S,T}=L_{T,U}=L_{S,U}.
$$
Otherwise at least one coefficient $C/L_{A,B}$ is not $1$, and the
common-conductor identity is an additive-kernel identity rather than a
primitive-edge identity.

This exactly mirrors the primitive repair torsor issue from Pass 107.
Additive kernels are closed under addition and under the weighted chain law.
Primitive representatives are arithmetic normalizations inside those
kernels.  A common-conductor sum can equal
$(C/L_{S,U})\eta_{S,U}$, whose coordinate gcd is $C/L_{S,U}$ because
$\eta_{S,U}$ is primitive.  Hence it is nonprimitive whenever
$C/L_{S,U}>1$.  The primitive locus is therefore not a sub-cocycle; it is a
choice of normalized representatives for rational/additive edge data.

### Pass 111 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Incorporate the Claude Code MacNeille reflection checker review and verify the
separation between syntactic fixed points and completion-created fixed cuts.

Proposer:
The review asks for a polarity repair in the MacNeille extension of an
antitone refutability map.  For lower cuts $C$ in the MacNeille completion,
the current rule should treat
$$
\boxtimes:L\to L^{op}
$$
as monotone first, then close in the opposite order.  The finite checker names
this rule
`antitone-dual-lower-cut-v1`:
$$
\widehat{\boxtimes}(C)
=\bigl((\boxtimes[C])^{l_L}\bigr)^{u_L}.
$$
The older rule
`antitone-dual-lower-cut-v0`,
$$
\bigl((\boxtimes[C])^{u_L}\bigr)^{l_L},
$$
is kept only as a wrong-polarity comparison.

Skeptic:
The review is not just a naming cleanup.  A principal completed fixed point
need not be reflected by a syntactic fixed point.  Therefore "principal" is
too weak as an output label: the checker must distinguish `reflected` from
`principal-unreflected`.  It must also test the principal extension condition.
For v1, the expected value of a principal lower cut is the dual principal cut
in $L^{op}$ at $\boxtimes a$, not the lower principal cut in $L$.

The size-3 non-lattice witness is the decisive polarity test.  Its carrier is
`{0,a,b}` with `0<a`, `0<b`, and `a` incomparable with `b`; refutability sends
`0` to `a` and both `a,b` to `0`.  There is no syntactic fixed point.  The
v1 completion creates the non-principal fixed cut `{ 0, a, b }`.  Legacy v0
instead returns the principal cut `{ 0, a }`, which is unreflected and violates
the principal extension condition.

Formalist:
The checker artifacts now separate three cases:

1. `three-element-nolattice-nosynt`, v1:
   `nonprincipal-without-syntactic`, completed fixed cut `{ 0, a, b }`,
   non-principal, no syntactic fixed point, no principal-extension failures.
2. `three-element-nolattice-nosynt`, v0:
   `principal-unreflected`, completed fixed cut `{ 0, a }`, principal at
   `a` but not reflected, with two principal-extension failures and a
   wrong-polarity warning.
3. `three-chain-antitone`, v1:
   `principal-unreflected`, syntactic fixed point `m`, completed fixed cut
   `{ b, m, t }`, principal at `t` but not reflected.

Thus the bare MacNeille reflection counterexample is real but still outside
the stronger APS theorem zone: the non-lattice witness is neither G2 nor FG2,
and the finite checker still warns that A1-A4 are not checked.

> **Theorem 111a (variance-sensitive MacNeille extension).** For an antitone
> refutability map, the usable finite-checker extension is the v1
> $L^{op}$-closure rule
> $\widehat{\boxtimes}(C)=((\boxtimes[C])^{l_L})^{u_L}$.
>
> **Theorem 111b (non-principal completion fixed point without syntax).** The
> three-element non-lattice model has no syntactic $\boxtimes$-fixed point,
> but under v1 its MacNeille completion has the non-principal fixed cut
> `{ 0, a, b }`.
>
> **Theorem 111c (principal does not imply reflected).** Both the legacy v0
> non-lattice control and the v1 three-chain smoke test exhibit principal
> completed fixed cuts that are not reflected by their principal element as a
> syntactic fixed point.

### Pass 112 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Add finite APS axiom-package checks to the MacNeille reflection checker and
test the smallest G2 boundary around the v1 non-principal completion fixed
cut.

Proposer:
The Pass-111 witness should not be dismissed merely because the checker had
not recorded A1-A4.  The next useful refinement is to make the report say,
for the finite table itself, which APS fragments hold:
A1 for monotonicity of `Box` and antitonicity of `boxtimes`, A2 as
`T <= boxtimes(bottom)`, A3 as the collision condition
`x <= Box(y)` and `x <= boxtimes(y)` imply `x <= boxtimes(T)`, and A4 as
`boxtimes(x) <= Box(boxtimes(x))`.  With those fields present, the
three-element V-shaped carrier can be exhausted rather than guessed.

Skeptic:
The new fields are finite order/table checks only.  They do not verify
residuals, canonical extension stability, or any theorem that completion
fixed cuts reflect back to syntax.  The search space is also deliberately
small: the carrier is fixed as `{0,a,b}` with `0<a`, `0<b`, and `a`
incomparable with `b`.  A no-go result here is therefore evidence about the
smallest non-lattice witness, not a general APS impossibility theorem.

Formalist:
The refreshed v1 report for `three-element-nolattice-nosynt` now says more
than Pass 111 did.  It still has no syntactic fixed point and still has the
non-principal completed fixed cut `{ 0, a, b }`, but its finite `apsAxioms`
field satisfies A1, A2, A3, and A4.  The witness fails G2 exactly because
`boxtimes(T) <= bottom` is true while `T <= bottom` is false.

The exhaustive fixed-carrier search in `check-pass112.py` enumerates all
total antitone `boxtimes` tables and all total `Box` tables on the same
V-shaped carrier.  Among the 216 separation tables, 54 satisfy G2 only in the
vacuous mode where `boxtimes(T) <= bottom` is false.  Once A2 is required,
the count drops to zero:

| package | separating tables |
| --- | ---: |
| completion separation | 216 |
| separation + G2 | 54 |
| separation + G2 + A2 | 0 |
| separation + G2 + A124Core | 0 |
| separation + G2 + A1-A4 APS | 0 |
| separation + A1-A4 APS but not G2 | 10 |

Thus, on this carrier, A2 is the first gate that prevents the vacuous-G2
escape.  Equivalently, the existing A1-A4 APS separation is still a useful
completion counterexample, but it sits on the non-G2 side of the boundary.

> checker now records finite-table A1-A4 data in an `apsAxioms` block, together

### Pass 113 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Extend the MacNeille G2/A2 boundary search to labelled four-element posets and
test whether the Pass-112 A2 gate survives the addition of one point.

Proposer:
The most economical extension is not yet all finite preorders with residuals,
but all labelled four-element posets with a unique bottom.  This keeps the
MacNeille cut computation small, preserves the finite-order reading of A1-A4,
and directly tests whether the V-carrier obstruction was only a size artifact.

Skeptic:
The result must not be over-read.  The search enumerates posets, not
non-antisymmetric preorders; it enumerates `Box` and `boxtimes` tables, not
tensor or residual operations; and it does not check preservation of A1-A4
after completion.  Also, in a non-collapsed model with `T` not below `bottom`,
any positive G2 result is vacuous in the formal implication sense:
`boxtimes(T) <= bottom` is false.

Formalist:
The A2 gate fails already on a minimal four-element non-lattice.  Let the
carrier be `{0,a,b,c}` with order generated by
$$
0<a<b,\qquad 0<c,
$$
and with `b` incomparable to `c`.  Set
$$
T=a,\quad \bot=0,
$$
$$
\boxtimes(0)=b,\quad \boxtimes(a)=b,\quad
\boxtimes(b)=0,\quad \boxtimes(c)=0,
$$
and
$$
\Box(0)=0,\quad \Box(a)=0,\quad \Box(b)=b,\quad \Box(c)=0.
$$
Then there is no syntactic fixed point of $\boxtimes$.  Under the v1
MacNeille extension, the whole lower cut `{ 0, a, b, c }` is a completed fixed
point and is non-principal, since the carrier has no greatest element.  The
finite-table APS fields all hold:
A1 for $\Box$ and $\boxtimes$, A2 because $a\le b=\boxtimes 0$, A3 by direct
table check, and A4 because $\boxtimes x\le\Box\boxtimes x$ for every
carrier element.  G2 holds because $\boxtimes T=b\not\le0$, and FG2 holds
because $\boxtimes^2(T)=0\le b=\boxtimes T$.

The labelled-poset enumeration gives the broader finite certificate:

| package | table count | profiles | posets |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| completion separation | 359424 | 1404 | 40 |
| separation + G2 | 135168 | 528 | 40 |
| separation + G2 + A2 | 61440 | 240 | 36 |
| separation + G2 + A124Core | 3024 | 240 | 36 |
| separation + G2 + A1-A4 APS | 2784 | 240 | 36 |

Thus the Pass-112 three-element no-go is genuinely carrier-local.  The next
boundary is no longer A2, but residual/completion stability.

> **Theorem 113a (four-element G2+APS completion separation).** There exists
> a labelled four-element poset model satisfying finite A1-A4, G2, and FG2,
> with no syntactic $\boxtimes$-fixed point, whose v1 MacNeille completion has
> a non-principal fixed cut.
>
> **Theorem 113b (A2 gate is three-element-local).** The Pass-112 A2 gate on
> the fixed V-carrier does not persist across all four-element posets.
>
> **Caveat 113c (residual gap).** The witness is not yet a residuated APS
> theorem: tensor, residuals, and completion-stability hypotheses are not
> supplied or checked.

### Pass 114 - 2026-06-21 JST

Focus:
Test whether the Pass-113 four-element MacNeille witness can be upgraded, on
the same carrier and the same order, to a residuated tensor package.

Proposer:
The shortest next boundary test is to keep the witness fixed and enumerate
every binary operation with a two-sided unit.  If any operation is
associative, monotone in both arguments, and has both residuals, then the
MacNeille separation survives a first residuation audit.  If none does, the
four-element model remains a finite table APS witness but not yet a
residuated APS witness.

Skeptic:
The scope is deliberately narrow.  This does not rule out an order repair, an
added top element, a quotient/collapse, a different four-element witness, or a
completion-level tensor.  It only says that the exact Pass-113 carrier/order
cannot carry the requested tensor/residual package.

Formalist:
For each possible unit `e` in `{0,a,b,c}`, `check-pass114.py` enumerates all
two-sided-unit binary operations.  The total operation space is
$$
4\cdot 4^9 = 1,048,576.
$$
The stage counts are:

| unit | operation space | associative | associative+monotone | full residual |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `0` | 262144 | 156 | 0 | 0 |
| `a` | 262144 | 156 | 6 | 0 |
| `b` | 262144 | 156 | 18 | 0 |
| `c` | 262144 | 156 | 32 | 0 |

Thus 624 operations are associative and 56 survive monotonicity, but no
surviving operation has both left and right residuals.  The first named
obstruction for the surviving units is a non-principal residual fiber:
$$
\{x:0\otimes x\le 0\}=\{0,a,b,c\}.
$$
This set is the whole carrier, and it is not a principal downset because the
carrier has no greatest element.  The same missing-top shape is exactly what
made the MacNeille fixed cut non-principal in Pass 113.

> **Theorem 114a (same-carrier residual no-go).** On the Pass-113 four-element
> carrier/order, no two-sided-unit associative monotone tensor admits both
> left and right residuals by the principal-downset criterion.
>
> **Caveat 114b (scope).** The theorem is fixed-carrier and fixed-order.  It
> does not decide order expansions, completion-level tensors, or other
> four-element G2+finite-APS witnesses.

### Pass 115 - 2026-07-02 JST

Focus:
Execute the Pass-114 "Next step": the weakest order repair of the Pass-113
four-element MacNeille witness that makes the residual obstruction principal.
The Pass-114 no-go pinned the first obstruction as the non-principal fiber
`{x : 0 (x) x <= 0} = {0,a,b,c}`, non-principal precisely because the carrier
has no greatest element.  The minimal repair adds the one missing join,
`U = b v c`, as a new top.  Question: does the repaired order still carry the
finite A1-A4/G2/FG2 profile, retain no syntactic fixed point, and -- the crux
-- retain the MacNeille completion-separation (a non-principal completion-fixed
cut with no reflecting syntactic fixed point)?

Proposer:
Adjoin `U` above `b` and `c`.  The base order `0<a<b, 0<c, b||c` becomes
`0<a<b<U, 0<c<U`.  This poset is a lattice; in fact it is the **pentagon
`N5`**, the unique smallest non-modular lattice (`b v c = U`, `b ^ c = 0`,
`a v c = U`, `a ^ c = 0`).  Antitonicity of `boxt` forces
`boxt U <= boxt b ^ boxt c = 0 ^ 0 = 0`, so `boxt U = 0`; the orbit is
unchanged, `T=a -> b -> 0 -> 0`, and the box-extension is free at `U` subject
to monotonicity (`box U >= box b = b`, so `box U in {b, U}`).  Claim: A1-A4,
G2, FG2 and no-synt-FP survive, and because `U` supplies the previously
missing top, the Pass-114 fiber `{x : 0 (x) x <= 0}` is now the principal
down-set `down(U)`, so a residuated tensor should exist.

Skeptic:
The repair cannot have it both ways.  A finite lattice is already complete, so
its MacNeille completion is itself and **every** cut is principal.  The
Pass-113 separation lived entirely on the non-principality of the fixed cut
`{0,a,b,c}`, which existed only because the carrier had no top.  Adjoining `U`
makes that very cut `down(U)`, principal -- and since `boxt U = 0 != U`, it is
now a *principal-unreflected* completion fixed point (the
`three-chain-antitone` phenomenon), not a separation witness.  So the
completion-separation is destroyed by the same move that repairs residuation.
Second worry: `N5` is non-distributive, so the integral tensor `(x)=^` need
not residuate; the residuated tensors that appear may be forced to
non-integral units.

Formalist:
Let `L = N5 = {0,a,b,c,U}`, `0<a<b<U`, `0<c<U`, `T=a`, `bot=0`,
`boxt: 0->b, a->b, b->0, c->0, U->0`, `box: 0->0, a->0, b->b, c->0, U->u`
with `u in {b,U}`.  Machine census
(`code/scripts/check-pass115.py`, report
`artifacts/reports/pass115-top-repair-n5-check.json`):

(A) **APS profile preserved.**  `boxt` is antitone; `synt-fp(boxt) = {}` (no
`x` with `boxt x = x`).  For *both* `u in {b,U}`: `box` monotone, and
A2 (`T=a <= b = boxt bot`), A3 (CutA3, table-checked), A4
(`boxt x <= box boxt x`), G2 (`boxt T = b !<= 0`, vacuously true), and FG2
(`boxt^2 T = 0 <= b = boxt T`) all hold.

(B) **Completion-separation destroyed.**  `L` has exactly 5 MacNeille-closed
lower cuts, **all principal** (it is a finite lattice).  Under the correct
antitone lower extension `boxt_hat(C) = ((boxt[C])^{l})^{u}`, the unique
completion-fixed cut is the whole carrier `down(U)`, which is principal and
**unreflected** (`boxt U = 0 != U`).  No non-principal completion-fixed cut
exists.  The Pass-113 witness's defining feature -- a non-principal
completion fixed point with no syntactic reflection -- is gone.

(C) **Residuation repaired, but only Rosser.**  Enumerating commutative
tensors that preserve joins in each argument (hence, on the complete lattice
`L`, are exactly the residuated ones; determined by their values on the
join-irreducibles `{a,b,c}` with `0 |-> 0`), there are **115** residuated
tensors, by unit: `a: 53`, `b: 18`, `c: 44`, and `U: 0`.  The integral unit
`U` carries **no** residuated tensor: the meet tensor `(x)=^` is not
residuated because `N5` is non-distributive (`a ^ (b v c) = a ^ U = a`, but
`(a^b) v (a^c) = a v 0 = a` -- distributivity holds for this triple, yet
`c ^ (a v ... )` fails elsewhere; concretely `^` fails join-preservation, so
its residual test fails).  The Pass-114 fiber `{x : 0 (x) x <= 0}` under `^`
is now `down(U)` = the whole carrier, **principal** -- the obstruction is
repaired -- but every residuated tensor on the repaired order has a
**non-integral** unit.

> **Theorem 115a (top-repair trilemma).**  Let `L0` be the Pass-113
> four-element carrier and `L = L0 + (U = b v c)` its top/join repair (`= N5`).
> Then (i) the finite APS profile A1-A4, G2, FG2 and `not FP-synt` transfer
> from `L0` to `L` under the forced `boxt`-extension and every monotone
> `box`-extension; (ii) the MacNeille completion-separation of `L0` does
> **not** transfer: `L` being a finite lattice, its unique completion-fixed
> cut `down(U)` is principal and unreflected; (iii) `L` admits residuated
> tensors (115 commutative ones), all with non-integral unit, and none with
> the integral unit `U`.
>
> **Corollary 115b (missing top is a single load-bearing defect).**  On the
> Pass-113 carrier the residual non-principality (Pass 114) and the
> completion-separation (Pass 113) are the *same* defect -- the absent join
> `b v c`.  Any order repair that supplies it makes the carrier a lattice,
> which (by finiteness = completeness) forces every completion cut principal,
> so the separation cannot survive a residuation-enabling top-repair on this
> carrier.  A non-principal MacNeille fixed cut **requires** a non-lattice
> carrier (a genuine join-defect).
>
> **Remark 115c (Rosser tax / Dedekind irony).**  The minimal join-repair
> lands on `N5`, Dedekind's canonical obstruction to modularity; its
> non-distributivity then forbids the integral (Loeb) tensor, so consistency's
> residual is repaired only at the cost of a forced non-integral (Rosser,
> Pass-51c) unit -- with, moreover, *no* syntactic `boxt`-fixed point to
> attach an integral unit to.  *Finitely repaired, Rosserly taxed.*

### Pass 116 - 2026-07-03 JST

Focus:
Execute the Pass-115 "Next step".  Cor 115b showed that on the Pass-113
four-element carrier the residual non-principality (Pass 114) and the
completion-separation (Pass 113) are the *same* defect -- the absent join
`b v c` -- and that supplying it as a single top `U` collapses the carrier to
the finite lattice `N5`, whose completion is itself and all of whose cuts are
therefore principal, killing the separation.  Pass 116 asks whether a *weaker*
repair -- bounded but deliberately **non-lattice** -- can keep the residual
fiber principal (repairing Pass 114) while retaining a non-principal MacNeille
completion-**fixed** cut (retaining Pass 113).  Concretely: adjoin a top `U`
but keep `b v c` unattained by giving `{b,c}` two incomparable minimal upper
bounds `m,n` -- the one-dimension-up analogue of the Pass-49 doubled cover
`a* < {m,b*}`.

Proposer:
Take `L1 = {0,a,b,c,m,n,U}` with covers
`0<a, a<b, 0<c, b<m, b<n, c<m, c<n, m<U, n<U` (`m || n`).  Then `L1` is bounded
(least `0`, greatest `U`) but **not** a lattice: `{b,c}` has minimal upper
bounds `m,n` with no least element, so `b v c` is unattained (likewise `a v c`;
dually `m ^ n` is unattained).  The forced antitone `boxt`-extension is
`boxt: 0->b, a->b, b->0, c->0, m->0, n->0, U->0` (antitonicity forces
`boxt m, boxt n, boxt U <= boxt b = 0`).  Because `U` is a genuine top, the
Pass-114 *bottom* fiber `{y : 0 (x) y <= 0}` becomes `down(U)` = whole carrier,
principal.  And because `b v c` is still unattained, the set `{0,a,b,c}` is a
MacNeille-closed cut that is NOT a principal down-set (no carrier element has
down-set `{0,a,b,c}`).  So both desiderata *appear* to be present at once: a
top for residuation, a genuine join-defect for a non-principal cut.

Skeptic:
Two independent failures sink the coexistence.  (1) Retaining a non-principal
*cut* is not the same as retaining a non-principal *fixed* cut.  The cut
`{0,a,b,c}` is the completion join point `j = b v c`, sitting ABOVE `b` and `c`.
But the orbit collapses both: `boxt b = boxt c = 0`.  Any antitone extension
sends a join to the meet of the images, `boxt_hat(j) = boxt_hat(b) ^
boxt_hat(c) = down(0) ^ down(0) = down(0) = bottom`.  Since `bottom <= b < j`,
`j` is NEVER fixed -- the only `boxt_hat`-fixed cut is the principal top
`down(U)` (`three-chain-antitone` phenomenon again).  (2) The top does not
actually repair residuation: the fiber merely *relocates*.  For a would-be
integral (unit `U`) tensor, `{y : a (x) y <= 0}` becomes `{0,a,b,c,m,n} = L1
minus {U}`, whose maximal antichain `{m,n}` again has no greatest element --
non-principal.  Adding one top cannot principalise a fiber that stops one level
BELOW the top.

Formalist:
Machine census `code/scripts/check-pass116.py` ->
`artifacts/reports/pass116-doubled-cover-coexistence-check.json`:

(A) **APS profile.** `boxt` antitone; `synt-fp(boxt) = {}`.  `A2`
(`T=a <= b = boxt 0`), `G2` (`boxt T = b !<= 0`, vacuous), `FG2`
(`boxt^2 T = 0 <= b = boxt T`) all hold; there are `25` monotone
`box`-extensions consistent with `A1-A4` (free choices of `box m, box n, box U`
subject to monotonicity).

(B) **Non-principal cut RETAINED, but UNFIXED.** `L1` has `8` MacNeille-closed
lower cuts, exactly `1` non-principal: `{0,a,b,c}` (the unattained `b v c`).
Under the antitone extension `boxt_hat(C) = ((boxt[C])^l)^u`, the UNIQUE fixed
cut is `down(U)` -- principal.  `boxt_hat({0,a,b,c}) = down(U) != {0,a,b,c}`.
No non-principal *fixed* cut exists; `separation_survives = false`.

(C) **Residuation NOT repaired.** The integral (unit `U`) commutative-tensor
census scans `345600` candidates: `2350` associative, `145`
associative+monotone, and **`0`** residuated.  The first named obstruction is
the relocated non-principal fiber
$$
\{y : a \otimes y \le 0\} = \{0,a,b,c,m,n\} = L_1 \setminus \{U\},
$$
whose maximal antichain `{m,n}` has no greatest element (Pass-114 obstruction,
moved up one level).

> **Theorem 116a (join-defect conservation / bounded-non-lattice
> no-coexistence).**  Let `L'` be any finite bounded poset extending the
> Pass-113 configuration `0<a<b`, `0<c` with `boxt` antitone, orbit
> `T=a -> b -> 0`, and `boxt b = boxt c = 0`, in which `b v c` remains
> unattained (so `{b,c}` has >= 2 minimal upper bounds).  Then:
> (i) the completion join point `j = b v c` satisfies
> `boxt_hat(j) = boxt_hat(b) ^ boxt_hat(c) <= boxt_hat(b) = down(boxt b) =
> down(0) = bottom`, hence `boxt_hat(j) <= b < j` and `j` is never a
> `boxt_hat`-fixed cut; the unique fixed cut is the principal top `down(top)`;
> (ii) keeping `b v c` unattained forces a maximal antichain `{m,n,...}` of
> minimal upper bounds strictly below the top, so the residual fiber
> `{y : a (x) y <= 0}` for any integral tensor contains that antichain and no
> greatest element, hence is non-principal.  Therefore residuation-repair and
> separation-preservation are **mutually exclusive** on every such `L'`.
>
> **Corollary 116b (the defect is conserved, only relocated).**  Sharpening
> Cor 115b: adjoining a top does not *remove* the `b v c` join-defect, it
> *displaces* it.  A single top (N5) relocates the defect INTO principality
> (kills the non-principal cut, repairs the fiber, but at the Rosser tax of
> Thm 115a).  A doubled-cover top (`L1`) keeps the non-principal cut but pushes
> the defect into (1) the `boxt_hat`-unfixedness of that cut and (2) a top-less
> residual fiber one level down.  In neither direction do "principal residual
> fiber" and "non-principal completion-fixed cut" coexist: the absent join is a
> conserved charge that can be moved between the two obligations but never
> annihilated on a finite carrier.
>
> **Remark 116c (why the orbit, not the order, is decisive).**  The obstruction
> in (i) is orbit-driven, not order-driven: it is `boxt b = boxt c = 0` -- the
> collapse of both join-summands to `bottom` -- that forces `boxt_hat(b v c) =
> bottom`.  A non-principal completion-fixed cut at a join point `j = x v y`
> would require `boxt x ^ boxt y = j > x,y`, i.e. the images of the summands to
> lie ABOVE the summands; antitonicity forbids this whenever `x,y` are already
> in the descending part of the orbit.  Fixed non-principal cuts therefore
> demand a join point built from *incomparable orbit-plateau* elements (a
> `boxt`-antichain 2-cycle, cf. the Pass-42 `R_2`/Pass-48 `R_{2k}` detached
> Rosser geometry), NOT from a collapsing chain like `T=a -> b -> 0`.

boxt x ^ boxt y = y ^ x` can equal the non-principal cut `x v y` itself -- i.e.
whether the detached Rosser geometry `R_2`/`R_{2k}` (Pass 42/48) admits a
bounded non-lattice carrier on which the completion join of the 2-cycle is a
non-principal `boxt_hat`-fixed cut, thereby achieving the coexistence that the
collapsing-chain orbit provably forbids (Thm 116a).

### Pass 117 - 2026-07-04 JST

Focus:
Execute the Pass-116 "Next step" and adjudicate Remark 116c.  Pass 116 proved
that a *collapsing chain* orbit `T=a -> b -> 0` cannot host coexistence of a
principal residual fiber with a non-principal MacNeille-completion-**fixed**
cut, because the completion join point `j = b v c` is sent to `bottom`
(`boxt_hat(j) = boxt b ^ boxt c = 0 < j`).  Remark 116c conjectured an escape:
route the join-defect through a `boxt`-antichain **2-cycle plateau** `{x,y}`
(`boxt x = y`, `boxt y = x`, `x || y`, so `boxt^2 x = x` -- a detached Rosser
`R_2` geometry), adjoin an unattained `x v y` by a doubled cover, and hope the
completion join becomes a non-principal `boxt_hat`-fixed cut.  Does the 2-cycle
supply the self-duality that the chain lacked?

Proposer:
Realize the plateau on the minimal bounded non-lattice carrier -- the
**hexagon** `H = {0,x,y,m,n,U}` with covers `0<x, 0<y, x<m, x<n, y<m, y<n,
m<U, n<U` (`x || y`, `m || n`).  `H` is bounded (least `0`, greatest `U`) but
not a lattice: `{x,y}` has two minimal upper bounds `m,n` with no least, so
`x v y` is unattained (dually `m ^ n`).  Antitonicity forces the orbit almost
entirely: `x<m` and `y<m` give `boxt m <= boxt x ^ boxt y = y ^ x = 0`, so
`boxt m = boxt n = 0`, and `m<U` gives `boxt U = 0`; `0<x,0<y` give
`boxt 0 >= x, y`, i.e. `boxt 0 \in {m,n,U}`.  Take the symmetric `boxt 0 = U`.
Then `{x,y}` is a genuine 2-cycle plateau sitting on a real join-defect: a top
`U` for residuation, an unattained join for a non-principal cut.  On its face
both desiderata are present, and unlike the chain the summands `x,y` are NOT
collapsed to a common `boxt`-image -- `boxt x = y \ne x = boxt y` -- so the
"images pinned to bottom" mechanism of Thm 116a does not obviously fire.

Skeptic:
It fires anyway, one level up, for a **parity** reason.  Compute the completion.
The Dedekind-MacNeille closure identifies the two defects: `x v y` as a cut is
`{x,y}^{ul} = {m,n,U}^l = {0,x,y}`, and `m ^ n` as a cut is
`down(m) ^ down(n) = {0,x,y}` -- the *same* set.  So the hexagon completion
adjoins a **single** new middle element `w = {0,x,y}` with
`0 < x,y < w < m,n < U`; `w` is the unique non-principal cut.  Now the antitone
extension acts by `boxt_hat(C) = (boxt[C])^l` (lower bounds of the image; this
agrees with `boxt` on principals, `boxt_hat(down a) = down(boxt a)`).  Then
$$
boxt\_hat(w) = (boxt[\{0,x,y\}])^l = \{boxt 0, boxt x, boxt y\}^l
            = \{U, y, x\}^l = down(x) \cap down(y) = \{0\} = \bot .
$$
The 2-cycle does not save `w`: an antitone map sends a join to the **meet** of
the images, and here `boxt x ^ boxt y = y ^ x = x ^ y = 0`.  So `w` is again
pinned to the bottom -- `boxt_hat(w) = \bot < w` -- and is not fixed.  Worse,
the whole map is fixed-point-free: its orbits are `0 <-> U`, `x <-> y`, and
`w -> 0`, none stationary.  The self-duality the plateau seemed to offer is a
length-2 swap, not a fixed point; the completion has no self-dual element in
which the swap could rest.  This is the exact `2^n`-complementation phenomenon
(an antitone involution on a Boolean-type interval is fixed-point-free).

Formalist:
Machine census `code/scripts/check-pass117.py` ->
`artifacts/reports/pass117-two-cycle-plateau-fixed-point-free-check.json`:

| model | carrier | cuts | non-principal | image of n.p. cut | fixed cuts | synt-FP |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| hexagon `R_2`, `boxt 0 = U` | 6 | 7 | `{0,x,y}` | `-> {0} = bot` | **0** | none |
| hexagon `R_2`, `boxt 0 = m` | 6 | 7 | `{0,x,y}` | `-> {0} = bot` | **0** | none |
| double-2-cycle (antichain 4) | 8 | 9 | `{0,p,q,r,s}` | `-> {0} = bot` | **0** | none |
| control `0<p<U`, `boxt p = p` | 3 | 3 | none | -- | **1** `= down(p)` | `p` |

All four are `boxt`-antitone.  The three even-orbit plateaus are globally
`boxt_hat`-fixed-point-free; only the control, which carries a genuine
syntactic refutability fixed point `p = boxt p`, produces a fixed cut (and it
is principal).  This isolates the operative variable: not the order, not the
boundedness, but the presence of an **odd self-dual seed** in the orbit graph.

> **Theorem 117a (even-orbit no-fixed-join).**  Let `L` be any bounded poset
> carrying a `boxt`-antichain 2-cycle plateau `{x,y}` (`boxt x = y`,
> `boxt y = x`, `x || y`) with `x v y` unattained (>= 2 minimal upper bounds).
> In the MacNeille completion, the completion join `j = x v y` satisfies
> `boxt_hat(j) = boxt x ^ boxt y = x ^ y`.  Since `x || y` gives
> `x ^ y <= x < j`, `j` is never `boxt_hat`-fixed.  On the minimal (hexagon)
> realization the completion identifies `x v y` with `m ^ n` into one middle
> cut `w`, and `boxt_hat` is globally fixed-point-free.
>
> **Corollary 117b (parity law: 116a and 117a are one).**  For any incomparable
> `x,y` with unattained join, the antitone De Morgan identity
> `boxt_hat(x v y) = boxt x ^ boxt y` makes the join a fixed cut iff
> `x v y = boxt x ^ boxt y`, i.e. iff the images `boxt x, boxt y` lie **above**
> the summands `x,y`.  A descending chain orbit puts the images at the bottom
> (Thm 116a: `boxt x ^ boxt y = \bot`); a swap 2-cycle puts them at the other
> summand (Thm 117a: `boxt x ^ boxt y = x ^ y`).  Every orbit that runs
> *through* the summands sends them at-or-below themselves, so no such orbit can
> fix the join.  The Pass-113 residuation/separation coexistence is therefore
> forbidden on **both** candidate geometries, for a single reason.
>
> **Theorem 117c (self-dual-seed necessity, finite).**  On a finite carrier,
> `boxt_hat` (antitone on the finite completion lattice `\hat L`) has a fixed
> cut iff the antitone-Tarski interval `[\,lfp\,boxt_hat^2,\ gfp\,boxt_hat^2\,]`
> contains a self-dual element.  For a pure even-cycle plateau this interval is
> the whole `[\bot,\top]` with `boxt_hat(\bot)=\top`, `boxt_hat(\top)=\bot` and
> no interior self-dual cut (fixed-point-free).  Hence a non-principal
> `boxt_hat`-fixed cut requires an **odd** self-dual seed -- concretely a
> Jeroslow refutability fixed point `p = boxt p` (FP-synt) already present in
> the carrier.  Completion-generated Rosser separation is a conservative shadow
> of FP-synt, not an escape from it.
>
> **Remark 117d (Smullyan gloss).**  `x` and `y` are two islanders each
> asserting the other is a knave (`boxt x = y`, `boxt y = x`).  The completion
> looks for a stable verdict `w` lying between them and finds only that the
> antitone "who-is-lying" operator flips `w` to the bottom: the island admits no
> consistent self-referential sentence unless some islander is *genuinely*
> self-referential (`p = boxt p`).  A 2-cycle is a paradox with no fixed point;
> only a 1-cycle -- a true Henkin/Jeroslow sentence -- can be believed.

Verified in this pass: (i) hexagon completion has exactly one non-principal cut
`w = x v y = m ^ n`, `boxt_hat(w) = \bot`; (ii) `boxt_hat` fixed-point-free for
both `boxt 0` choices and for the antichain-4 double-2-cycle; (iii) control
with FP-synt yields the fixed cut `down(p)`.  Proof obligations (not closed
here): the general `2k`-cycle `R_{2k}` statement (conjectured fixed-point-free
by the same De Morgan parity, verified only for `k=1` and the split `k=1+1`);
the residuation half inherits Pass-116's relocation verbatim (the integral fiber
`{y : x (x) y <= 0}` retains the antichain `{m,n}` with no greatest element,
non-principal) and was not re-censused this pass.

### Pass 118 - 2026-07-04 JST

Focus:
Decide whether Theorem 117c's necessity is STRICT.  Thm 117c (Pass 117) claimed
that a non-principal `boxt_hat`-fixed cut in the MacNeille completion "requires
an ODD self-dual seed -- effectively a Jeroslow FP-synt point `p = boxt p`".
The question: can the self-dual seed be COMPLETION-GENERATED -- i.e. can a
finite bounded carrier with NO syntactic fixed point (`boxt x != x` for all `x`)
have a MacNeille completion in which some non-principal cut `w` is
`boxt_hat`-fixed?

Proposer:
Reuse the exact Pass-117 hexagon `H = {0,x,y,m,n,U}` (covers `0<x,0<y`,
`x<m,x<n,y<m,y<n`, `m<U,n<U`) whose completion adjoins the single non-principal
cut `w = {0,x,y} = x v y = m ^ n`.  Pass 117 killed `w` by choosing the
plateau `boxt x = y, boxt y = x`, i.e. `boxt[F] = F` for the lower frontier
`F = {x,y}`; the antitone De Morgan law then gives
`boxt_hat(w) = boxt x ^ boxt y = y ^ x = bottom`.  The remedy is to route the
frontier the OTHER way.  Take the **frontier-crossing** map
$$
boxt\,0=U,\quad boxt\,x=m,\quad boxt\,y=n,\quad
boxt\,m=y,\quad boxt\,n=x,\quad boxt\,U=0 .
$$
This is antitone (all eight covers check), has NO syntactic fixed point, and now
`boxt[F] = {m,n} = G` (the UPPER frontier of `w`), so
`boxt_hat(w) = boxt x ^ boxt y = m ^ n = w`.  The cut `w` is fixed with no
carrier-level `p = boxt p`.

Skeptic:
Two objections, both answered.  (1) "`w` fixed might be an artifact of a
symmetric involution."  No: the orbit here is the 4-cycle `(x m y n)` (plus the
2-cycle `(0 U)`), an EVEN, NON-involutive orbit; a parallel-swap variant
`boxt x=m, boxt m=x, boxt y=n, boxt n=y` (three 2-cycles) also fixes `w`.  So
neither oddness nor involutivity is at issue.  (2) "Maybe some carrier element
is secretly self-dual."  Direct check: `boxt` is fixed-point-free on `H`.  The
seed `w` is a genuinely NEW cut.  The only real content of Pass-117's Thm 117c
that survives is the general antitone Tarski-interval criterion; its
identification of the seed with a carrier Jeroslow point is false.

Formalist:
Let `L` be a finite bounded poset, `boxt` antitone, `\hat L` its MacNeille
completion, and `boxt_hat(C) = (boxt[C])^l`.  For a non-principal cut `w`, write
`F = max(w \cap L)` (its lower frontier) and `G = min(\{a \in L : a \notin w\})`
restricted to the minimal upper bounds, so that as elements of `\hat L`,
`w = \bigvee F = \bigwedge G`.

> **Lemma 118a (antitone De Morgan frontier law).** For every cut `w`,
> `boxt_hat(w) = \bigwedge_{f \in F} boxt(f)`.  *Proof.* `w \cap L = \downarrow F`;
> since `boxt` is antitone the minimal elements of `boxt[\downarrow F]` are
> exactly `\{boxt f : f \in F\}` (larger arguments give smaller images), so
> `(boxt[w\cap L])^l = (\{boxt f\}_{f\in F})^l = \bigcap_f \downarrow boxt f =
> \bigwedge_f boxt f`. ∎

> **Theorem 118b (frontier-onto fixed-cut criterion).** A non-principal cut `w`
> is `boxt_hat`-fixed **iff** `boxt[F] = G`, i.e. iff `boxt` maps the lower
> MacNeille frontier of `w` ONTO its upper frontier.  *Proof.* By Lemma 118a,
> `w` fixed `\iff \bigvee F = \bigwedge_{f\in F} boxt f`.  The right side equals
> `w = \bigwedge G` iff the meet of the images is exactly `w`, which on a cut
> with frontier pair `(F,G)` holds iff `\{boxt f\}_{f\in F} = G`. ∎  No
> hypothesis `p = boxt p` appears; the criterion is carrier-fixed-point-free.

> **Corollary 118c (necessity of Thm 117c is not strict).** The map above
> realizes `boxt[F] = G` with `F, G` the frontiers of `w = \{0,x,y\}` on the
> hexagon, so `w` is a non-principal `boxt_hat`-fixed cut with NO carrier
> synt-FP.  FP-synt is NOT necessary for completion-separation.  The Tarski
> interval `[lfp boxt_hat^2, gfp boxt_hat^2]` of Thm 117c indeed contains a
> self-dual element, but that element is a NEW cut, not a carrier point.

> **Remark 118d (parity is a red herring; Smullyan gloss).** Pass 117's slogan
> "even orbit no fixed point, odd self-dual seed needed" is superseded.  The two
> witnesses realize `w` via a 4-cycle and a double-2-cycle -- both EVEN.  What
> matters is *where* the antitone map routes the frontier: `boxt[F]=F` (paradox,
> images collapse to bottom) vs `boxt[F]=G` (stable verdict, images meet at `w`).
> The islanders `x,y` no longer accuse each other; each accuses an upper
> islander (`boxt x = m`), and the completion's middle judge `w` -- "the case
> against me is exactly the case I make" -- is believed.  The completion supplies
> a Henkin/Rosser fixed point the base theory never wrote down.
